topics.title: Topological sort
topics.subtitle: Order dependent tasks by repeatedly removing work with no prerequisites.
topics.summary: A topological ordering places every directed edge u → v with u before v. Kahn’s algorithm tracks each node’s incoming-edge count, queues the nodes with zero prerequisites, and reduces the count of their dependents as it processes them. If fewer than all nodes are processed, a cycle prevents a valid ordering.
principles: Model each prerequisite as a directed edge from prerequisite to dependent task.
Initialize indegree from incoming edges and enqueue every zero-indegree node.
When removing a node, decrement each neighbor’s indegree and enqueue it exactly when that count reaches zero.
A valid order contains every node; if the processed count is smaller, the graph has a cycle.
Adjacency lists make the algorithm O(V + E) in time and space.

frames.caption: A and B are prerequisites for C, and C is a prerequisite for D. Count each incoming edge.
Only A and B have no unmet prerequisites, so both can begin the ordering.
Remove A. C still has one prerequisite, so it is not ready yet.
Remove B. C now has no remaining prerequisites and joins the queue.
Removing C unlocks D. Processing every node proves the graph is acyclic.
frames.state: order = [A, B, C, D] · O(V + E)

questions.title: Course Schedule
questions.prompt: Decide whether all courses can be completed given prerequisite pairs.
questions.why: Build prerequisite edges and run Kahn’s algorithm. If the processed node count equals the number of courses, no prerequisite cycle blocks completion.

frames.caption: Prerequisites 0→1, 1→2, and 2→1 leave 1 and 2 in a cycle.
Courses 0 and 3 are initially available; processing them cannot unlock the cycle.
The queue is empty while two courses remain, so those courses cannot be completed.

questions.title: Course Schedule II
questions.prompt: Return one valid order in which to take all courses, or an empty list if impossible.
questions.why: Append a course to the answer when it leaves the zero-indegree queue. The final list is valid exactly when it contains every course.

frames.caption: Courses 0 and 1 have no prerequisites; either may appear first.
Take 0. Its outgoing prerequisite edge reduces course 2’s indegree.
Take 1; now 2 is unlocked. Completing 2 later unlocks 3.
Every course appears once and each prerequisite precedes its dependent course.

questions.title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
questions.prompt: Find each recipe that can be produced from the initial supplies and other producible recipes.
questions.why: Treat each ingredient as a prerequisite for its recipe. Start with available supplies; when an ingredient becomes available, decrement the dependent recipe counts and enqueue newly unlocked recipes.

frames.caption: Flour is already available, so it satisfies one dependency of bread.
Yeast is also supplied; bread reaches zero missing ingredients and becomes available.
Bread and ham satisfy the sandwich recipe, unlocking it in turn.

topics.title: Dijkstra and weighted paths
topics.subtitle: Expand the best known route first and relax its outgoing edges.
topics.summary: For nonnegative edge weights, Dijkstra’s algorithm settles the smallest tentative distance first. Relaxing an edge means replacing a neighbor’s distance when the route through the current node is better. A priority queue selects the next candidate; stale entries are skipped. Unlike ordinary BFS, this handles edges with different costs.
principles: Initialize the source distance to zero and all others to infinity; push (0, source) into a min-heap.
Pop the smallest candidate. Skip it if its cost is larger than the node’s best recorded distance.
Relax each outgoing edge with candidate = distance + weight; push only strict improvements.
A target can be returned when popped with its current best distance, not when first discovered. Negative edges invalidate the settling argument.
With lazy heap entries, the general bound is O((V + E) log(V + E)) time and O(V + E) space. Other monotone path objectives can use the same best-first structure.

frames.caption: Start at S. Edges are S→A:4, S→B:1, B→A:2, A→T:1, B→T:7.
Set tentative distances from S; B is cheaper and will be popped first.
Through B, improve A from 4 to 3 and discover T at cost 8.
Pop A at cost 3 and improve T to 4. The old (4,A) entry is stale and gets skipped.
Pop T at its best cost. The route S→B→A→T costs 1+2+1=4.
frames.state: answer = 4 · discovery alone did not settle T

questions.title: Network Delay Time
questions.prompt: Return the earliest time at which every node receives a signal from the starting node, or −1 if any node is unreachable.
questions.why: Run Dijkstra on directed nonnegative travel times. The answer is the maximum finite shortest distance; return −1 if any node remains at infinity.

frames.caption: Source 2 sends along edges 2→1:1, 2→3:1, 3→4:1.
Relax both outgoing edges of source 2. Nodes 1 and 3 receive the signal at time 1.
Settling node 3 unlocks node 4 at time 2.
All nodes are reachable. The slowest shortest arrival determines the answer.

questions.title: Path With Minimum Effort
questions.prompt: Move through a height grid and minimize the largest absolute height difference along the route.
questions.why: Replace additive relaxation with candidate = max(effort_so_far, abs(height[u] − height[v])). Taking another edge cannot lower the current effort, so the minimum-effort heap candidate can be settled safely.

frames.caption: Grid rows are [1,2,2], [3,8,2], [5,3,5]. The top/right route ends with a jump of 3.
Explore the left side: jumps 1→3 and 3→5 are both 2.
Continue 5→3→5; both jumps are 2, so the route effort stays 2.
When the target is popped at effort 2, no smaller-effort route remains pending.

questions.title: Path with Maximum Probability
questions.prompt: Find the path with the largest product of edge success probabilities, returning zero if the destination is unreachable.
questions.why: Start the source probability at 1 and use a max-heap (negative probabilities with Python heapq). Relax by multiplication and keep larger values. Since probabilities are in [0,1], extending a path cannot improve its product.

frames.caption: Discover node 1 with probability 0.5 and node 2 with probability 0.2.
Through node 1, improve node 2 because 0.5×0.5 exceeds 0.2.
Pop node 2 with probability 0.25. Returning when it was first discovered would have been incorrect.

topics.title: Binary search on the answer
topics.subtitle: Turn an optimization problem into a monotone feasibility check.
topics.summary: Instead of looking for an element in a sorted array, search a range of possible answers. Define feasible(x) so it changes from false to true at one boundary. To find the minimum feasible answer, test the midpoint and discard half the candidate range. The main work is proving monotonicity and building a correct feasibility check.
principles: State the decision question first: can this speed, capacity, or day satisfy the constraints?
Prove that a feasible candidate stays feasible as the candidate increases; otherwise this first-true search does not apply.
Choose a lower bound and a guaranteed feasible upper bound, handling impossible inputs before searching.
Use while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if feasible(mid), set hi = mid; otherwise set lo = mid + 1. Return lo.
If a feasibility scan costs O(n), searching a candidate range of width R costs O(n log R), usually with O(1) extra scan space.

frames.caption: Suppose candidates 1–4 fail and 5–8 succeed. We seek the first success without scanning them all.
frames.state: feasible = F F F F T T T T · lo=1, hi=8

frames.caption: Test midpoint 4. Failure proves every candidate at most 4 is too small.
Test 6. Success keeps 6 as a possible answer but discards larger candidates.
Test 5, which also succeeds; preserve the smallest feasible boundary.
The bounds meet at 5. No lower candidate can be feasible.

questions.title: Koko Eating Bananas
questions.prompt: Find the smallest integer eating speed that finishes all piles within h hours.
questions.why: At speed k, required hours are sum((pile+k−1)//k). More speed cannot increase hours. Search from 1 to max(piles); the upper bound works because the problem guarantees at least one hour per pile.

frames.caption: For h=8, test speed 6: the four piles require 1,1,2,2 hours.
Test speed 3: the hours are 1,2,3,4, so speed 3 is too slow.
Speed 5 needs 1+2+2+3=8 hours, so keep [4,5].
Speed 4 also needs 1+2+2+3=8 hours. Bounds meet at 4.

questions.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
questions.prompt: Find the minimum ship capacity that sends packages in their given order within the allowed days.
questions.why: Greedily pack each day until the next package would exceed capacity, then start a new day. This minimizes days for that capacity. More capacity cannot require more days. Search from max(weights) to sum(weights); never sort the packages.

frames.caption: Allow 3 days. Capacity 4 produces loads [3],[2,2],[4],[1],[4].
Capacity 6 produces loads [3,2],[2,4],[1,4].
Capacity 5 produces loads [3,2],[2],[4,1],[4].
Feasibility switches between capacities 5 and 6, so 6 is the minimum.

questions.title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
questions.prompt: Find the earliest day to make m bouquets of k adjacent, non-overlapping bloomed flowers.
questions.why: Reject m*k > n. For each candidate day, scan the garden: reset the run on an unbloomed flower, and consume each run of k bloomed flowers as a bouquet. Waiting longer never removes usable flowers. Search between the minimum and maximum bloom days.

frames.caption: Need m=2 bouquets with k=3. At day 7, the unbloomed center flower splits runs of length 4 and 2.
On day 11 the same gap remains. Six bloomed flowers alone do not prove two adjacent bouquets exist.
At day 12 all seven flowers bloom. One run can supply two disjoint groups of three.
Use indices [0,1,2] and [3,4,5]; the earliest feasible day is 12.

topics.title: Monotonic deque
topics.subtitle: Keep only useful candidates and remove them from either end.
topics.summary: A monotonic deque stores candidate indices in an order that makes the best candidate available at the front. Remove expired candidates from the front and dominated candidates from the back. Unlike a monotonic stack, it supports both candidate expiry and dominance removal, making moving-window extrema and certain prefix-sum problems linear.
principles: Store indices so you can test whether a candidate has left the valid range.
For a window maximum, maintain decreasing values: a later value at least as large dominates an earlier smaller value because it also expires later.
For a window minimum, reverse the value ordering. Two deques can track a window’s maximum and minimum together.
Each index is appended once and removed at most once, giving O(n) total deque operations. Python collections.deque supports popleft() without shifting an entire list.
Choose front-removal rules from the problem: expiry for fixed windows, completed answers for shortest prefix-sum differences. Prove why every removed candidate is no longer needed.

frames.caption: With window size 3, indices 0 and 1 remain candidates in decreasing value order.
Value 3 dominates the older 2: pop index 1 from the back, then append index 2.
When the window moves to indices 1–3, index 0 expires from the front.
Value 5 dominates both remaining candidates, so remove them from the back.
The three windows have maxima 4, 3, and 5; candidates never need to be rescanned.

questions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.prompt: Return the maximum value in every contiguous window of size k.
questions.why: Before reading the answer, expire indices smaller than the window start. Pop smaller or equal values from the back, append the new index, and read nums[deque[0]] once the first complete window exists.

frames.caption: At right=2, value 3 has already dominated 1. The deque holds indices [1,2].
Append −3. The front is still within the window and remains its maximum.
At right=4, index 1 expires. Value 5 removes the remaining smaller candidates.
Continue expiry and dominance removal for each new window.

questions.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
questions.prompt: Find the longest contiguous subarray whose largest and smallest values differ by at most limit.
questions.why: Use a decreasing deque for maxima and an increasing deque for minima. While max−min exceeds the limit, move the left boundary and expire candidates. Record the largest valid window length; each index enters and leaves each deque at most once.

frames.caption: With limit=4, begin with a singleton, which always satisfies the difference constraint.
Adding 2 makes max−min=6. Move left past 8 and expire index 0.
Add 4: the new window has minimum 2 and maximum 4.
Adding 7 makes [2,4,7] invalid. Remove 2; [4,7] is valid.

questions.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
questions.prompt: Find the shortest nonempty subarray with sum at least k, allowing negative values; return −1 if none exists.
questions.why: Build prefix sums P and maintain indices with strictly increasing prefix values. For current j, pop front indices while P[j]−P[front]≥k, updating length j−front. Pop back indices while P[j]≤P[back]: the newer prefix is at least as good for every future endpoint and yields a shorter interval.

frames.caption: For nums=[2,−1,2] and k=3, the displayed values are prefix sums P=[0,2,1,3], not the original array.
Prefix index 1 has value 2; retain it after the initial zero.
Prefix value 1 at index 2 dominates value 2 at index 1. It is smaller and later.
At prefix index 3, P[3]−P[0]=3. Record length 3 and remove front 0; the next difference is only 2.

topics.title: KMP and the prefix function
topics.subtitle: Reuse matched prefixes instead of restarting after a mismatch.
topics.summary: The prefix table pi[i] records the length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also its suffix. When a new character mismatches, fall back from length j to pi[j−1] until a shorter border can extend. KMP uses this table to search text without moving the text pointer backward, taking O(n+m) time for text length n and pattern length m.
principles: A proper prefix excludes the entire string; prefix and suffix occurrences are allowed to overlap.
Build pi left to right: start j=pi[i−1]; while j>0 and s[i]!=s[j], set j=pi[j−1]; increment j on a match, then assign pi[i]=j.
During search, j is the length of the pattern prefix matching the text suffix read so far. On mismatch, follow prefix-table links before comparing the same text character again.
When j equals the pattern length, the match starts at i−m+1. To find overlapping matches, continue with j=pi[m−1].
Each successful extension increases j by one and each fallback decreases it, giving linear total work. The pattern table uses O(m) extra space.

frames.caption: Build pi for ababaca. Through index 4, the longest border is aba, length 3.
At i=5, c does not match s[3]=b. Fall back using pi[2]=1.
c also mismatches s[1]=b, so fall back to pi[0]=0. It mismatches a too.
At i=6, a extends the length-zero border by one.
Every fallback uses a previously proven border; no prefix needs to be rescanned from scratch.

questions.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
questions.prompt: Return the first position of needle inside haystack, or −1 if no occurrence exists.
questions.why: Build the prefix table for needle and scan haystack with one matched-length pointer. A mismatch changes only that pointer through failure links; the text position never retreats.

frames.caption: Search needle=ababac in haystack=abababac. After text index 4, five pattern characters match.
Text index 5 is b but needle[5] is c. Fall back to pi[4]=3, then match that same b against needle[3].
The next a matches needle[4].
The final c completes all six pattern characters.

questions.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
questions.prompt: Decide whether the string consists of two or more copies of a shorter substring.
questions.why: Let L=pi[n−1] and candidate period p=n−L. Repetition exists exactly when L>0 and n%p==0. A border alone is insufficient unless the candidate period tiles the full length.

frames.caption: For ababab, build the border lengths for every prefix.
The longest proper border is abab, length L=4.
The candidate block ab tiles all six characters exactly three times.
Contrast aba: its border length is 1, but candidate period 2 does not divide length 3.
frames.state: a nonempty border alone does not prove repetition

questions.title: Longest Happy Prefix
questions.prompt: Return the longest nonempty prefix that is also a proper suffix, or an empty string when none exists.
questions.why: Compute the prefix function once and return s[:pi[n−1]]. The table directly answers the longest-border question, including overlapping prefix and suffix occurrences.

frames.caption: At prefix aba, a is both prefix and suffix, giving pi[2]=1.
At prefix abab, ab is a border of length 2.
At the end, prefix abab equals suffix abab beginning at index 2. Overlap is allowed.
Return the first four characters. The full string is excluded by the proper-prefix definition.

topics.title: Merge sort and cross-half counting
topics.subtitle: Sort smaller ranges, then count relationships while merging.
topics.summary: Merge sort divides a contiguous range in two, recursively sorts each half, and merges them with two pointers. Sorted halves also let you count relationships between their elements in linear time. Each index pair belongs to one recursive split, so internal-half counts plus cross-half counts cover all pairs without duplication.
principles: Use half-open ranges [lo,hi); a range of length zero or one is already sorted.
Merge sorted halves by taking the smaller front value, then append either remaining tail. A reusable buffer avoids repeated allocation.
Preserve original indices when answers belong to original positions; sorting only the values loses that association.
For strict smaller-than counts, merge equal left values first so equal right values do not contribute.
Prove the pair-count condition separately from the merge comparison. Each level does O(n) work, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary buffer space plus O(log n) recursion depth.

frames.caption: Split the contiguous input into [5,2] and [6,1]. Every original left index precedes every original right index.
Recursively sort the left half and count its single ordinary inversion: 5>2.
Sort the right half and count 6>1.
During merge, right value 1 precedes both remaining left values 2 and 5: two cross-half inversions.
Finish the merge as [1,2,5,6]. The original array has four ordinary inversions.

questions.title: Sort an Array
questions.prompt: Sort the integer array in ascending order without using a built-in sort, meeting O(n log n) time.
questions.why: Recursively sort each contiguous half, merge through a shared buffer, then copy the merged range back. Merge sort gives a predictable O(n log n) bound with O(n) auxiliary space; discuss heapsort if the interviewer requires constant auxiliary space.

frames.caption: Split into [5,2] and [3,1], then recurse down to single elements.
Merge the left singleton ranges by selecting 2 before 5.
Merge the right singleton ranges by selecting 1 before 3.
Merge [2,5] with [1,3]: take 1,2,3, then the remaining 5.

questions.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
questions.prompt: For each original position, count values strictly smaller than it to its right.
questions.why: Merge (value, original_index) pairs. Whenever a right value is emitted before a left value, increment a moved-right counter. Add that counter when emitting each left value. Equal values take from the left first. Recursive internal counts and cross-half counts accumulate at original indices.

frames.caption: Sorting [5,2] adds one to the answer for original index 0.
Sorting [6,1] adds one to the answer for original index 2.
Merge sorted halves [2,5] and [1,6]. Emit 1, then 2; one right-side value is smaller than 2.
Emit 5 with moved-right count 1, adding its cross-half smaller value.

questions.title: Reverse Pairs
questions.prompt: Count original index pairs i<j for which nums[i] is greater than twice nums[j].
questions.why: After sorting both halves, scan left values in ascending order and advance a right pointer while left>2*right. Add how many right values qualify for each left value, then perform a normal merge. The counting pointer never retreats. Python integers avoid overflow; fixed-width languages need a wider type for doubling.

frames.caption: Split at index 2: left [2,4] and right [3,5,1]. Count internal pairs recursively.
The sorted halves are [2,4] and [1,3,5]. Count cross pairs before the final normal merge.
For left value 4, only right value 1 qualifies. The next value 3 fails because 4≤6.
Add internal and cross counts, then merge the sorted ranges.

topics.title: Fenwick tree and dynamic prefix sums
topics.subtitle: Update a point and query a prefix in logarithmic time.
topics.summary: A Fenwick tree stores overlapping power-of-two blocks of an array. In its one-based internal representation, tree[i] covers lowbit(i)=i&−i elements ending at i. A prefix query jumps left with i-=lowbit(i); a point addition updates every covering block with i+=lowbit(i). This supports changing sums or frequency counts in O(log n) per operation.
principles: Convert external zero-based positions to one-based internal indices; index zero is only a stopping sentinel, never an update position.
prefix(i) sums internal positions 1 through i. An external inclusive range [l,r] is prefix(r+1)−prefix(l).
For assignment, compute delta=new−old and add delta to all covering tree blocks; keep the old values separately.
A frequency tree can count values below a coordinate. Compress arbitrary values into sorted ranks while preserving equality.

Each operation visits O(log n) blocks using O(n) storage. The subtraction trick requires an invertible aggregate such as sum; this basic structure does not directly support arbitrary range minimum with arbitrary point replacements.

frames.caption: Displayed numbers are internal indices. Node 6 covers [5,6], while node 4 covers [1,4].
To query prefix 6, take tree[6], covering positions 5 and 6.
Next take tree[4], covering 1 through 4, then stop at zero. The blocks are disjoint.
To add delta at position 5, update nodes 5,6,8: each stored block includes position 5.
Queries decompose a prefix; updates repair its containing blocks. Neither scans all array elements.
frames.state: O(log n) per add or prefix query

questions.title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
questions.prompt: Support point assignments and inclusive range-sum queries on a changing array.
questions.why: Initialize a Fenwick tree from the array, retain the current values, and translate update(index,val) into add(index+1,val−old). Compute sumRange(l,r) as prefix(r+1)−prefix(l). Building by repeated adds takes O(n log n); each subsequent operation takes O(log n).

frames.caption: Initial values are [1,3,5]. The one-based tree stores [1,4,5] at nodes 1–3.
Assign external index 1 the value 2. This is an addition of −1 at internal position 2.
Update tree[2] from 4 to 3; the next ancestor is 4, outside this three-element tree.
prefix(3) takes tree[3]+tree[2], totaling 5+3.

questions.title: Create Sorted Array through Instructions
questions.prompt: Insert values in order and sum the smaller of the counts strictly below and strictly above each inserted value, modulo 1,000,000,007.
questions.why: Maintain frequencies by value or compressed rank. Before inserting x, less=prefix(rank−1) and greater=inserted_count−prefix(rank), excluding equals from both sides. Add min(less,greater), then increment x’s frequency.

frames.caption: Insert 1 into an empty frequency tree. Both strict-side counts are zero.
For 5 there is one smaller and no greater value. Insert 5 after querying.
For 6 there are two smaller and no greater values.
For 2, only 1 is smaller while 5 and 6 are greater.

questions.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key
questions.prompt: For each requested value, return its current zero-based position in the permutation and move it to the front.
questions.why: Reserve q empty positions before the initial m values. Store occupancy 1 for each value’s current position. Its current rank is prefix(position−1). Remove its old occupancy and place it in the next unused front slot. This avoids physically shifting the permutation and costs O((m+q) log(m+q)); a simple list also suffices for the original small constraints.

frames.caption: With queries [3,1,2,1], reserve four front slots. Initial values occupy internal positions 5–9. Query 3 at position 7.
Move 3 to slot 4. Value 1 at slot 5 now has one occupied slot before it.
frames.state: query 1 → rank=1 · move it to slot 3

frames.caption: Value 2 remains at slot 6. Slots 3 and 4 are occupied before it.
frames.state: query 2 → rank=2 · move it to slot 2

frames.caption: Value 1 at slot 3 now follows only the occupied slot 2. Move it to slot 1.

topics.title: Sweep line and boundary events
topics.subtitle: Process changes at boundaries instead of revisiting every interval.
topics.summary: A sweep line turns intervals into start and end events, sorts the event coordinates, and maintains the state between consecutive boundaries. Additive state needs only net deltas; an active maximum needs a heap or ordered multiset. Group events at the same coordinate before reporting the new state so touching intervals are handled consistently.
principles: Choose interval semantics first: [l,r) stops at r, while an inclusive integer range [l,r] can be represented by removal at r+1.
For sums or occupancy, add weight at the start and subtract it at the end; a running total reconstructs the active load.
Group all events at a coordinate before evaluating the state immediately to its right; avoid spurious intermediate changes.
For a skyline, track active heights with multiplicities or a heap with expiry. Removing one building must not remove another building of the same height.
With sparse coordinates, sort O(n) boundaries for O(n log n) processing. A dense bounded coordinate range may use a difference array and a linear scan.

frames.caption: Two half-open weighted intervals are [1,5) with weight 2 and [3,7) with weight 3. Only the four boundaries change the load.
At coordinate 1 the load becomes 2 and remains 2 until coordinate 3.
At coordinate 3 add 3; the intervals now overlap.
At coordinate 5 remove 2, leaving only the second interval.
At coordinate 7 remove 3. The sweep is complete without inspecting interior coordinates.

questions.title: Car Pooling
questions.prompt: Decide whether a vehicle can serve every trip without exceeding its capacity, dropping passengers before picking up new ones at the same location.
questions.why: Create +passengers at pickup and −passengers at dropoff. Aggregate deltas by location, sweep in ascending order, and reject if the resulting occupancy exceeds capacity. Half-open trips allow seats freed at a stop to be reused there.

frames.caption: Trips [2,1,5] and [3,3,7] begin with two passengers at location 1.
At location 3, three more passengers board.
For capacity 5, the same trips are possible. Two passengers leave at location 5.
The final three leave at location 7. Aggregating a drop and pickup at one stop avoids a false overflow.

questions.title: Corporate Flight Bookings
questions.prompt: Return the total reserved seats on each flight after bookings that add seats across inclusive flight-number ranges.
questions.why: For a booking [first,last,seats], add seats at first and subtract at last+1. Prefix-sum the differences for flights 1 through n. This performs every range addition in constant time, then reconstructs the final totals in O(n+bookings) time.

frames.caption: Booking [1,2,10] contributes +10 at flight 1 and −10 at flight 3.
Booking [2,3,20] contributes +20 at flight 2 and −20 at flight 4.
Booking [2,5,25] adds 25 at flight 2; its removal is at sentinel flight 6.
Prefix-sum only the real flights, excluding the sentinel.

questions.title: The Skyline Problem
questions.prompt: Return the key points where the maximum active building height changes.
questions.why: Sweep all unique starts and ends. At x, push buildings starting there into a max-heap of (height,end), then pop top entries with end≤x until the top is live. The heap top is the visible height, or zero. Emit one point only when this height changes. Expired buried entries can wait until they reach the top.

frames.caption: Buildings are [2,9,10], [3,7,15], [5,12,12]. At x=2 the active maximum is 10.
At x=3, height 15 hides height 10. The building starting at 5 has height 12 and changes no visible height.
At x=7, the height-15 building expires, exposing height 12.
At x=9 height 10 expires while hidden; at x=12 the last building ends.
